Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette: At seventy-six, Dang still carries the physical weight of being a child in a war zone, not as a distant story, but as a present-tense memory. He was ten when the fighting reached his village, and the afternoon that changed his trajectory began with the sharp, acrid scent of burning rubber and damp earth. He had been helping his family stack supplies when armed men dragged them into the flooded field, pressing their faces into the mud. The weight of their knees on his back, the cold metal of a rifle barrel against his temple, and the muffled shouts of a struggle between two groups created a trap from which he felt he could not escape. He remembers every detail with unsettling clarity: the exact pattern of cracked clay beneath his palms, the way the light fractured through the dust clouds, the steady rhythm of boots shifting against the packed soil. Those moments did not fade. They settled into him, and over the decades, he learned that certain things in the present could pull them back without warning. Now working the night shift at a distribution warehouse outside Portland, Dang finds that the environment constantly tests the boundaries he has built. The warehouse is a labyrinth of steel racks, conveyor belts, and narrow service corridors. When a forklift backs into a tight alcove and the steel gate slams shut behind him, the sudden confinement of his shoulders against the corrugated wall sends his breath short. He is certain that the pressure means he is caught again, that escape is impossible until someone decides to move him. He steps back from the gate before his hands even shake, claiming equipment malfunction to the floor manager. These experiences exist alongside his daily routine. He avoids the loading bay during peak hours, takes longer routes through the main aisle, and leaves early when the diesel exhaust from the idling trucks drifts through the ventilation system. The smell arrives independently, immediate and absolute. It floods his chest without signaling anything else. He has come to believe that the air itself can betray him, so he keeps his respirator clipped to his belt, not for dust, but as a barrier he can pull up when the scent shifts. The memories do not announce themselves. They arrive fully formed, as if the past has simply stepped into the present. While unloading a crate of industrial solvents, a sharp chemical tang hits the back of his throat. In an instant, the warehouse floor drops away, replaced by the vivid, unbroken image of the burning field and the men's faces. The emotion rises so fast and so heavily that he has to stop. He sets the box down, closes his eyes, and breathes until his shoulders unclench. He does not fight the feeling or try to push it away; he simply waits for the wave to recede, knowing that forcing himself to continue would only deepen the disorientation. This has happened repeatedly, usually on the same side of the building where the ventilation pulls in the afternoon sun and the older trucks. He does not know why the memories surface without warning, only that they are always complete, always precise, and always demanding his full attention until they pass. These parallel experiences have quietly altered the shape of his days. He no longer volunteers for inventory audits that require close quarters with supervisors, and when arguments break out over shipping errors, he steps away rather than meet the tension. His coworkers have grown used to his distance, and he has grown used to theirs. A naturalized American who has lived in the Pacific Northwest for decades, he lives alone in a small apartment with the blinds drawn. He has stopped answering calls from old friends who ask about the past. The war is over, he tells himself, but the body remembers what the mind tries to quiet. What finally brought him to the clinic was a recent shift where the smell of burning plastic in the warehouse hallway triggered a full return, leaving him unable to finish his rounds or drive home. He fears losing the last of his independence, losing the ability to work, and losing the fragile calm he has managed to construct. He hopes the clinicians might help him understand why the past keeps walking back into his life, and whether he can learn to let it pass without stopping everything he does.
